checkpoints.prompt: A user logged in successfully, but only a specific S3 operation returned AccessDenied. Which layer should you check next?

choices.text: Evaluation of the principal, action, and resource for authorization
choices.explanation: When an operation is denied after identity has been verified, the next step is to examine the evaluation of the permission policies.

choices.text: Change the login password repeatedly
choices.explanation: Authentication has succeeded, so changing the password does not explain an authorization denial.

choices.text: Shorten only the DNS TTL
choices.explanation: DNS cache does not change the evaluation of IAM permissions for an operation.

choices.text: Make the S3 object public without restriction
choices.explanation: Using public access settings to work around an authorization problem violates least privilege.

checkpoints.title: Authentication and authorization are different questions

checkpoints.prompt: Choose one recommended design. The batch process needs S3 write permissions for only 3 hours.

choices.text: The batch principal assumes a role and runs with temporary credentials.
choices.explanation: Temporary role credentials limit access by purpose and duration, avoiding the distribution of long-term secret keys.

choices.text: Give every developer an administrator access key with no expiration.
choices.explanation: Credentials that are both permanent and overly privileged conflict with role-based and least-privilege design.

choices.text: Make the S3 bucket public anonymously so credentials are unnecessary.
choices.explanation: Anonymous public access does not restrict permissions and cannot allow only the intended writes.

choices.text: Hard-code credentials in the source code.
choices.explanation: Hard-coding secrets in code increases the risks of exposure and makes revocation harder to manage.

checkpoints.title: Principals and roles: Who temporarily becomes what?

checkpoints.prompt: An operation is denied even though the identity policy contains an Allow. Select the two things to check first during evaluation.

choices.text: Check whether there is an explicit Deny for the same principal/action/resource.
choices.explanation: An explicit deny takes precedence over an Allow, so the Allow alone is not enough to determine the outcome.

choices.text: Evaluate the effective permissions, including resource policies and conditions.
choices.explanation: Effective permissions are determined by the combination of multiple policies and conditions.

choices.text: Ignore Deny whenever there is an Allow.
choices.explanation: Ignoring an explicit Deny is an error in IAM evaluation.

choices.text: Allow all actions to resolve the denial.
choices.explanation: Overly broad Allow permissions undermine least privilege without identifying the cause.

checkpoints.title: Policy: Check for Deny as well as Allow

checkpoints.prompt: Choose two appropriate ways to reduce the permissions required by an image-processing Lambda function.

choices.text: Allow only the required prefixes and actions in the target bucket.
choices.explanation: Limiting resources and actions to what the task requires is the principle of least privilege.

choices.text: Issue temporary credentials to the execution role.
choices.explanation: Short-lived credentials limit the impact of a leak compared with long-term keys.

choices.text: Grant the image-processing function administrative permissions for all AWS services.
choices.explanation: Permissions for all services exceed the requirements of the task.

choices.text: Store the key indefinitely in a Lambda environment variable.
choices.explanation: Storing a long-term secret key forfeits the benefits of temporary credentials.

checkpoints.title: Least Privilege and Temporary Credentials

choices.text: Verify who the accessing entity is.
choices.explanation: Authentication verifies the identity of a person or entity.

choices.text: Allow operations on S3 objects.
choices.explanation: This is an authorization decision.

choices.text: Encrypt data.
choices.explanation: Encryption is a means of protecting data.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose one correct statement about authentication.
finalQuestions.title: Authentication

choices.text: Inspect only the password entry screen.
choices.explanation: Since you are already signed in, this may not be an authentication-only issue.

choices.text: Check the requested action, the target bucket, and the permissions policy.
choices.explanation: Look up the action and resource required for authorization.

choices.text: Change S3 to EBS.
choices.explanation: Changing the storage service does not help identify the cause of the denial.

finalQuestions.prompt: After signing in, you get AccessDenied for a specific bucket. Choose the one correct first step to investigate.
finalQuestions.title: Authorization failure

choices.text: Identity verification is strengthened, but permissions for S3 operations are still managed by policies.
choices.explanation: Multi-factor authentication strengthens identity verification. Authorization determines what a verified principal is allowed to do.

choices.text: Passing multi-factor authentication makes it possible to read from and write to every bucket.
choices.explanation: Stronger identity verification does not automatically grant permissions to perform actions on resources.

choices.text: Because authentication has been strengthened, policies for the target resources are no longer needed.
choices.explanation: Authentication and authorization address different questions, so permissions for actions on targets still need to be managed.

finalQuestions.prompt: You made multi-factor authentication mandatory at login. Choose the one correct statement that combines authentication and authorization.
finalQuestions.title: Distinguishing the stages

choices.text: An identity that grants permissions to the principal that assumes it.
choices.explanation: Roles have permission policies attached to them.

choices.text: It must always have a long-term password and long-term access keys.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Roles do not have long-term credentials.

choices.text: An AWS service can assume it.
choices.explanation: Services such as EC2 can also use roles.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose the one incorrect statement about IAM roles.
finalQuestions.title: Role

choices.text: Associate an IAM role with EC2 that grants only the S3 operations required.
choices.explanation: Grant the execution environment only the permissions it needs.

choices.text: The application uses temporary credentials from the role.
choices.explanation: This lets it run without embedding long-term keys.

choices.text: Write a long-term access key directly into the source code.
choices.explanation: This should be avoided. It goes against the design of using a role and temporary credentials.

finalQuestions.prompt: An application running on EC2 writes to a specific S3 bucket. Choose the one incorrect way of providing permissions.
finalQuestions.title: EC2 permissions

choices.text: Only human console actions have a principal; applications on EC2 have no acting entity.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. A principal is an entity that performs an action, and it is not limited to people. Even for a request made by an application on EC2 using a role’s temporary credentials, authorization checks which principal is acting.

choices.text: Grant permissions only after identifying which entity will act.
choices.explanation: Identifying the principal is the starting point.

choices.text: Do not share the same long-term key between a person and a running application.
choices.explanation: You can assign separate roles to each principal and use temporary credentials.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose the one incorrect statement about principals and roles.
finalQuestions.title: Understanding principals

choices.text: An explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow.
choices.explanation: An explicit denial takes precedence during evaluation.

choices.text: Finding one Allow means no other policies are needed.
choices.explanation: Deny statements and conditions must also be checked.

choices.text: Policies are unrelated to resources.
choices.explanation: Evaluation specifies the action and resource.

choices.text: When investigating, specify the principal, action, and resource.
choices.explanation: Evaluate the request with its details fixed.

choices.text: Deny applies only to encryption.
choices.explanation: Deny is part of access permission evaluation.

finalQuestions.prompt: Select two correct statements about IAM policy evaluation.
finalQuestions.title: Explicit Deny

choices.text: Grant administrator permissions without checking what the error applies to.
choices.explanation: This violates least privilege and does not identify the cause.

choices.text: Check whether the requested action and resource match an Allow.
choices.explanation: This checks for a mismatch with the target resource.

choices.text: Delete and recreate the S3 resource.
choices.explanation: This does not investigate policy evaluation.

choices.text: Ignore Deny if the request is authenticated.
choices.explanation: An explicit Deny takes precedence.

choices.text: Check for explicit Deny statements and conditions in the bucket policy and other policies.
choices.explanation: These may explain the denial even when an Allow exists.

finalQuestions.prompt: A read request is denied even though an Allow exists. Choose two correct investigation steps.
finalQuestions.title: Investigating AccessDenied

choices.text: The operation is denied.
choices.explanation: An explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow.

choices.text: It will always succeed because there is an Allow.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect because it ignores the Deny.

choices.text: Examine the policy and conditions that produce the Deny.
choices.explanation: This is the next step to narrow down the cause.

choices.text: The Deny will disappear if you authenticate again.
choices.explanation: Authenticating again does not remove a policy Deny.

choices.text: S3 does not evaluate policies.
choices.explanation: Access is evaluated using IAM, resource policies, and other mechanisms.

finalQuestions.prompt: Both an Allow for S3:GetObject and an explicit Deny for the same resource apply. Select two correct conclusions.
finalQuestions.title: Conclusion about the Allow

choices.text: Specify the required actions and resources.
choices.explanation: This is the starting point for narrowing the required scope.

choices.text: To make things work, grant administrator permissions for all resources from the outset.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. First determine the required scope.

choices.text: Separate roles according to what each principal needs.
choices.explanation: You can distinguish among people, CI, and applications.

choices.text: Share one long-term access key among everyone and every application.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. It undermines separation and traceability of principals.

choices.text: Review permissions based on actual usage.
choices.explanation: This helps you decide how to reduce excessive permissions.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose two statements about least privilege that are incorrect.
finalQuestions.title: Least privilege

choices.text: Always allow deletion from all buckets.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Limit permissions to the reads and writes that are needed.

choices.text: List the input and output bucket paths.
choices.explanation: This lets you specify the resource precisely.

choices.text: Grant the job role only the actions it needs.
choices.explanation: This is least privilege tailored to the principal.

choices.text: Consider a role that can use temporary security credentials.
choices.explanation: This can reduce the distribution of long-term keys.

choices.text: Copy a developer’s personal access key into the job configuration.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Keep personal credentials separate from the runtime environment.

finalQuestions.prompt: You are granting permissions to a daily CSV import job. Select the two incorrect methods.
finalQuestions.title: Daily job

choices.text: List the actions the process performs and the resources they target.
choices.explanation: This is the basis of least privilege.

choices.text: Assign separate roles to each execution identity.
choices.explanation: This clarifies permission boundaries.

choices.text: Allow all actions to avoid investigating failures.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. It broadens the impact.

choices.text: Put long-term keys with no expiration in shared configuration.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Consider temporary credentials.

choices.text: Verify actual access, including explicit denies and conditions.
choices.explanation: Confirm that only the intended scope is permitted.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose two statements that are incorrect as an approach to designing permissions for a new process.
finalQuestions.title: Permission design sequence

blocks.label: Overview
blocks.text: Consider identity verification, permissions, roles, and least privilege as distinct concepts.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Be able to distinguish authentication, authorization, IAM roles, and least privilege when evaluating configurations.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Distinguish authentication from authorization and explain which stage failed.

blocks.text: Explain how an IAM principal and a role obtain temporary permissions.

blocks.label: Authentication and authorization are different questions
blocks.text: Authentication verifies who the entity trying to access a resource is. Passwords, multi-factor authentication, and federation are ways to verify a person or entity.

blocks.label: Authorization determines which actions a verified entity is allowed to perform. If you can sign in but cannot read an S3 object, the issue lies with authorization after authentication.
blocks.text: When troubleshooting, first check whether authentication succeeded, then check whether access is allowed to the target resource and action. Do not treat “cannot sign in” and “access denied” as the same problem.

blocks.label: Authentication and authorization are different questions.
blocks.text: Authentication and authorization are different questions.

steps.label: Authentication and authorization are different questions.

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: The user can sign in to the console but cannot open the billing bucket.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Confirm that a successful sign-in means authentication succeeded.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Check the requested S3 operation and the target bucket.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Check which policy allows or denies the action.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Authentication has already been completed, so investigate this as an authorization issue.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If sign-in succeeds, you can operate all AWS resources.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Sign-in is authentication. Actual operations are authorized separately by policies.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Authentication verifies an identity.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Authorization grants permission to perform an action.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Identify the stage that failed, step by step.

blocks.label: Principals and roles: Who temporarily becomes what
blocks.text: A principal is an entity that can perform actions in AWS. IAM users, roles, AWS services, and federated users can all be principals.

blocks.label: An IAM role is an identity with a permissions policy. The entity that assumes the role uses the permissions defined for it through temporary credentials. The role itself has no long-term password or access keys.
blocks.text: When granting permissions to an application, first design which principal will assume which role before embedding access keys in a file. Assigning roles according to responsibilities helps limit access to the necessary period and scope.

blocks.label: Principals and roles: Who temporarily becomes what.

steps.label: An IAM role is an identity with a permissions policy. The entity that assumes the role uses the permissions defined for it through temporary credentials. The role itself has no long-term password or access keys.

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: An application on EC2 saves its output to a specific bucket.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: List only the S3 operations the application needs.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Create an IAM role with those permissions.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Attach a role to EC2, and have the application use temporary credentials.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can associate permissions with the runtime role without placing long-term access keys in the application configuration.

blocks.label: Incorrect
blocks.text: A role is a container that stores a person’s login password.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: A role is an assumable permission identity. It does not have long-term passwords or access keys.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A principal is the entity that performs an action.

blocks.label: A role is a permission-bearing identity that you assume and use.
blocks.text: A role uses temporary credentials.

blocks.label: Policies: Examine denials, not just permissions
blocks.text: IAM policies define the actions that a principal can perform on resources. During an investigation, determine specifically who is allowed to perform which actions on which resources.

blocks.label: Policies: Examine denials, not just permissions
blocks.text: Do not draw a conclusion merely because you find one permission. In IAM evaluation, an explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow. Therefore, check for applicable denials, including permissions boundaries, organization policies, and resource-based policies.

blocks.label: Policies: Examine denials, not just permissions
blocks.text: To investigate AccessDenied, fix the requesting principal, action, and resource; confirm the relevant Allow; then look for explicit Deny statements and conditions. Do not infer the cause solely from the displayed service name.

steps.label: Policies: Examine denials, not just permissions

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Identify the principal, s3:GetObject, and the key for the target bucket.

blocks.label: Step 2

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Check for explicit Deny statements and conditions in the bucket policy and other applicable policies.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: By checking for applicable Deny statements rather than just whether an Allow exists, you can correctly identify the reason for the rejection.

blocks.label: Least privilege and temporary credentials
blocks.text: Least privilege means allowing only the actions, resources, and conditions needed for the work. Instead of granting administrator permissions for all resources from the outset, observe the operations that are needed and narrow the scope.

blocks.label: Least privilege and temporary credentials
blocks.text: Temporary credentials are created dynamically and have an expiration time. They can be used with roles or federation, helping reduce the risks of distributing and storing long-term access keys.

blocks.label: Least privilege and temporary credentials
blocks.text: In an implementation, do not share the same credentials among people, CI, and running applications. Assign separate roles to each principal, and grant access only after checking the expiration, target resources, and required actions.

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: Grant permissions to a job that only performs daily CSV imports.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: List the input bucket to read from, the output bucket to write to, and the required actions.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Create a role policy limited to those actions and paths.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Associate a role with the job, and regularly review its actual usage.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can avoid granting unnecessary delete permissions or access to other buckets, while also limiting the impact of a leak.
